h1: The rules that define Irish whiskey
title: The Rules That Define Irish Whiskey | Craft Beer School
desc: What legally makes a whiskey Irish: made on the island of Ireland, three years in wood, 40% ABV and the four categories including single pot still.
teaser: Irish whiskey has its own rules and its own spelling. One category exists nowhere else.
standfirst: Irish whiskey is protected by law and by a technical file that sets out exactly how it must be made. Here is what those rules say, including the one category that makes Irish whiskey unique.
sections: Made anywhere on the island of Ireland

Irish whiskey must be distilled and matured on the island of Ireland. That includes both the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland, which is part of the United Kingdom. A whiskey made in Belfast and one made in Cork can both be Irish whiskey.

The name is protected as a geographical indication. The rules are set out in Irish law, in the Irish Whiskey Act 1980. They are set out in more detail in a technical file registered with the European Union.
Three years in wood, 40% in the bottle

The spirit must be distilled from a mash of malted cereals, with or without whole grains of other cereals. It must be distilled to less than 94.8% ABV so it keeps the flavour of the raw materials. It must then mature for at least three years in wooden casks on the island of Ireland and be bottled at a minimum of 40% ABV.

Notice the word wooden. Scotch must mature in oak. Irish rules allow other woods too, although oak is still what nearly every Irish distillery uses. As with Scotch, plain caramel colouring is allowed and the age on the label is the age of the youngest whiskey in the bottle.
Four categories, one of them unique

The technical file defines four categories:

  • Malt Irish whiskey: made only from malted barley, distilled in pot stills.
  • Grain Irish whiskey: made from malted barley with other cereals such as maize or wheat, distilled in column stills.
  • Pot still Irish whiskey: made from a mix of malted and unmalted barley, distilled in pot stills.
  • Blended Irish whiskey: a blend of two or more of the above.

Most Irish whiskey sold around the world is blended. The category that only Ireland has is pot still.
Single pot still is Ireland's own style

Pot still Irish whiskey, usually labelled single pot still when it comes from one distillery, must use a mash of at least 30% malted barley and at least 30% unmalted barley. Up to 5% other cereals, such as oats, are allowed.

The style grew out of the nineteenth century, when a tax on malt pushed distillers to use raw barley alongside it. Unmalted barley gives a distinctive spicy, oily, creamy texture that malted barley alone does not. Tasters often describe it as peppery with green apple and a thick mouthfeel. Our guide to single pot still Irish whiskey goes deeper into the style.

Many people believe Irish whiskey must be triple distilled. It does not have to be. Triple distillation is a strong Irish tradition and many distilleries use it. Some Irish malts are double distilled. The law allows both.

The same goes for peat. Most Irish whiskey is unpeated, but peated Irish whiskey exists and is perfectly legal. The rules control origin, raw materials, distillation strength, maturation and bottling strength. Flavour choices are left to the distiller.

Ireland and the United States usually spell it whiskey. Scotland, Canada, Japan and India usually spell it whisky. The difference is a matter of custom that settled in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. No law makes the e a requirement. A few producers break the pattern.

It is a useful clue on a shelf, not a guarantee. The category and the country on the label are what count.
Why grain whiskey matters in a blend

Grain Irish whiskey is made in column stills, which run continuously and produce a lighter spirit than pot stills. On its own it is soft and sweet, often with notes of cereal, vanilla and banana. In a blend it gives volume and a gentle base for the pot still or malt whiskey to sit on.

The legal minimum for each part of the blend is the same: three years in wood on the island. A blended Irish whiskey with an age statement of 12 years means the youngest component, grain included, is at least 12. That is often a better sign of quality than the word premium on the box.

Beer drinkers have a handy parallel. A column still grain whiskey is to a pot still whiskey what a light adjunct lager is to an all-malt beer. Lighter, cleaner and easy to drink, but carrying less of the raw material's character.
Taste pot still against a blend

The rules make most sense once you have tasted them. Pour 25 ml of a blended Irish whiskey and 25 ml of a single pot still side by side in tulip glasses. Nose each neat, then with a few drops of water. The blend will usually feel lighter and softer. The pot still will feel thicker and spicier. That difference is the unmalted barley you just read about.

Drink water alongside, pace yourself and never drink and drive. Naming textures and spice notes precisely is a skill you can train, much like reading a beer's body and bitterness.
Check one label against the four categories

Your first step: find one bottle of Irish whiskey and look for its category. Is it malt, grain, pot still or blended? If the label does not say, it is very likely a blend. Once you can sort Irish whiskey into those four boxes, every tasting note starts to make more sense.
faqs: How long must Irish whiskey be aged?
At least three years in wooden casks on the island of Ireland.
Does Irish whiskey have to be triple distilled?
No. Triple distillation is traditional and common, but double distilled Irish whiskey is also legal.
What is single pot still Irish whiskey?
Whiskey from one distillery made in pot stills from a mash of at least 30% malted and at least 30% unmalted barley.
Can whiskey from Northern Ireland be Irish whiskey?
Yes. The rules cover the whole island of Ireland, both the Republic and Northern Ireland.
